body.text: The striking development is not simply that China now has more space companies. It is that Beijing is giving them more room to compete while drawing them more deliberately into the country’s wider space ambitions.

China says more than 600 commercial space enterprises now operate across launch, satellite manufacturing and downstream applications such as communications, remote sensing and data services. In 2025, commercial space missions accounted for 50 of China’s 92 launches; they placed 311 commercial satellites into orbit. Yet only half of those missions used commercially developed launch vehicles.

That apparent contradiction is insightful. China’s commercial-space sector is not emerging as an alternative to the state program. It is becoming another way of delivering national space capability. The policy architecture makes that explicit.

Beijing also introduced its first dedicated commercial-space standards system. More than 1,000 standards are planned across six broad areas – spanning rocket and satellite manufacturing, launch and tracking, market access, licensing, safety, debris mitigation, certification and space-based services. The aim is not simply to achieve technical consistency; it is to create the operating rules for a much larger commercial space economy.

China is doing two things at once: encouraging space companies to become more entrepreneurial and international while building the rules needed to keep that expansion compatible with national priorities.

This is not privatisation in the familiar sense. Nor is it simply old-style state direction. It is an attempt to combine the speed and experimentation of competing commercial companies with the infrastructure, procurement and long-term objectives of a national program.

That matters because China needs much more launch capacity. Large satellite constellations, lunar exploration, human spaceflight and scientific missions all compete for launch opportunities. Multiple providers and reusable rockets could lower costs, increase cadence and make the system more resilient when individual vehicles fail.
But Beijing also wants its commercial companies to look outward.

The same action plan encourages them to expand overseas and help smaller space-faring nations build satellite applications. We have already seen an early example in Thailand. In August, Beijing-based commercial satellite company GalaxySpace delivered the Lingzhi-09 CubeSat to Thailand’s space agency, GISTDA, together with ground systems, training and technical support.

The company described it as the first complete in-orbit satellite delivery by a Chinese commercial space firm to a Southeast Asian customer. That may be the beginning of a more consequential export model.

For emerging space countries, that could widen the menu of available partners. If that model scales successfully, Chinese commercial companies could become an important interface between the country’s space capabilities and emerging markets. The significance would lie not only in selling satellites or launches but in supplying the training, software and technical relationships around them.
The policy challenge is that going global also means deciding what can travel with these companies, and what cannot.

The regulation makes clear that China wants companies to invest overseas while observing existing rules on export controls, technology transfer, cross-border data and security review. It specifically covers technology, services, data and even some forms of overseas technical training.
There is no evidence so far that Order No. 837 has blocked or materially altered a particular commercial-space deal. Its significance is more subtle.

That may prove to be the defining experiment in China’s commercial-space boom. The experiment therefore cuts both ways. Commercial firms gain room to move faster, attract capital and pursue overseas customers; Beijing gains additional capacity without abandoning coordination.
The question is no longer whether private companies can find a place in China’s space sector. They clearly can.
The question is how far they can become global commercial actors while remaining part of a coordinated national system.
